Dissolved oxygen (DO) is oxygen gas held in solution in water. The greatest DO concentration that seawater can hold when it is in equilibrium with the air, called the saturation concentration, depends on the water's temperature. For the salinity of the bay described here, the saturation concentration is 9.0 mg/L at 10 °C, 8.1 mg/L at 15 °C, 7.4 mg/L at 20 °C, and 6.7 mg/L at 25 °C. The percent saturation of a water sample is its DO concentration divided by the saturation concentration at the sample's temperature, multiplied by 100. Water with a DO concentration below 2.0 mg/L is called hypoxic; most fish and crabs cannot survive in hypoxic water for long.

In late summer, researchers lowered a probe from a boat at two stations in a coastal bay. Station A was in the open outer bay, 3 km from the mouth of a river. Station B was in the inner bay, 0.5 km from the river mouth and sheltered from the wind by a peninsula. At each station the probe recorded water temperature and DO concentration every 5 m from the surface to a depth of 30 m. At Station B the probe malfunctioned at a depth of 15 m, so no readings were recorded at that depth. Figure 1 shows DO concentration versus depth, and Figure 2 shows water temperature versus depth, at the two stations.

Activated charcoal removes dissolved dyes from water by adsorption: dye molecules stick to the charcoal's surface. Students measured the removal of a blue dye from water. In each trial, a flask containing 100 mL of a 50 mg/L dye solution was placed in a water bath at 25 °C and stirred, and a measured mass of powdered activated charcoal was added at time 0. At 10, 20, 30, 45, and 60 min, a 2 mL sample was withdrawn, passed through a filter with 0.45 µm pores, and placed in a spectrophotometer, which measured the sample's absorbance of light at a wavelength of 590 nm (the wavelength the dye absorbs most strongly). The dye concentration of each sample was determined from a calibration curve prepared from dye solutions of known concentration at pH 7. Percent removal was calculated as the percent of the original 50 mg/L that was no longer present in solution.

Experiment 1
Trials were performed at pH 7 with 0.5 g, 1.0 g, or 2.0 g of charcoal. The results are shown in Figure 1 (solid lines).

Experiment 2
Trials were performed with 1.0 g of charcoal in dye solutions adjusted to pH 3 or pH 11 by adding a few drops of hydrochloric acid or sodium hydroxide solution. The results are shown in Figure 1 (dashed lines). The students later found that, at the same dye concentration, a solution at pH 11 has an absorbance at 590 nm that is 15% lower than that of a solution at pH 7, and that the absorbance at pH 3 is the same as at pH 7.

Experiment 3
The charcoal from the 1.0 g trial at pH 7 was collected on a filter at 60 min, rinsed with 50 mL of water, dried at 105 °C, and added to a fresh 100 mL portion of 50 mg/L dye solution at pH 7. After 60 min, 61% of the dye had been removed. When the same charcoal was collected, rinsed, dried, and used a third time, 45% of the dye had been removed after 60 min.

In a species of mosquito, resistance to a widely used insecticide is conferred by a single allele, R, of a gene coding for an enzyme that breaks down the insecticide. R is dominant to the susceptible allele, S: mosquitoes of genotype RR or RS survive exposure to the insecticide, and SS mosquitoes are killed by it. In a population in which mating is random, if the frequency of the R allele is p and the frequency of the S allele is q = 1 − p, the fraction of the population with genotype SS is expected to be q², and the fraction that is resistant (RR or RS) is expected to be 1 − q².

A town at the western end of a river valley has sprayed the insecticide inside its houses every June for the past 12 years. The insecticide has never been used elsewhere in the valley. Because SS mosquitoes are killed during spraying, the frequency of R in the town rises sharply each June and then declines over the following months as mosquitoes move in from unsprayed areas. In one week in September, researchers set light traps overnight at six sites in the valley: at the town's edge (0 km) and at 2, 5, 10, 20, and 40 km east of the town along the river. From each site, 200 adult mosquitoes were collected and genotyped, and the frequency of the R allele was calculated as the number of R alleles divided by the total number of alleles (400 per site). Figure 1 shows the R allele frequency at each site.

Astronomers monitored the brightness of a Sun-like star, K-31, for five years. Every 11.3 days the star dims by a few percent for about 6 hours and then returns to its normal brightness. Four features of these dimming events are notable: (1) each event is deeper when the star is observed in blue light than when it is observed in red light; (2) the depth of the events has decreased gradually, from 4.0% in the first year of monitoring to 3.0% in the fifth year; (3) the interval between events has remained 11.3 days to within a few minutes; and (4) spectra of the star show no periodic Doppler shift larger than 5 m/s, the smallest shift the instruments can detect. Three scientists offer explanations.

Scientist 1
A planet orbits K-31 with a period of 11.3 days and passes in front of the star once each orbit. The planet is surrounded by an extended hazy atmosphere. The haze scatters blue light more strongly than red light, so the planet blocks more blue light and the events are deeper in blue. The planet's mass is small, so the Doppler shift it produces in the star's spectrum is below the detection limit. A second, more distant planet is slowly tilting the first planet's orbit, so that a shrinking fraction of the planet's disk crosses the star each orbit; this is why the events are becoming shallower.

Scientist 2
A cloud of dust orbits K-31 with a period of 11.3 days. The cloud is debris from a small icy body that broke apart. Dust grains scatter blue light more strongly than red light, which explains the color difference. The cloud's mass is far too small to move the star, so no Doppler shift is expected. The cloud is slowly spreading out along its orbit; a more spread-out cloud blocks less light at any one moment, which is why the events are becoming shallower.

Scientist 3
No body orbits K-31. The star rotates once every 11.3 days and carries a large dark spot, a cooler region of its surface. Each time rotation brings the spot into view, the star appears dimmer. Because a cooler surface emits proportionally less blue light than red light, the events are deeper in blue. The spot is gradually shrinking, so the events are becoming shallower. Spots of this kind drift slowly toward a star's equator, where the star rotates slightly faster, so the interval between events should shorten by several hours over the coming years.

A thin layer of tiny glass spheres (spherules) occurs in marine sedimentary rock at three sites in a coastal region. At all three sites the layer lies between the same two fossil-bearing limestone beds, so it was deposited at the same time everywhere. The spherules are 0.1 mm to 1 mm in diameter and are about 70% silica (SiO2) by mass. They contain about 2,000 parts per million (ppm) of nickel; typical rock of Earth's continental crust contains about 80 ppm. No grains of shocked quartz (quartz with the microscopic fracture planes produced only by extremely high pressure) have been found in the layer. A field of extinct volcanoes lies 300 km west of Site A, and a circular depression 4 km across, now buried under younger sediment, has been detected beneath the seafloor 20 km east of Site A. Two scientists discuss how the layer formed.

Scientist 1
The layer was produced by the impact of a nickel-rich meteorite. The impact melted the rock at the point of impact and sprayed molten droplets high into the atmosphere; the droplets became spheres as they cooled in flight and rained down over the region. The buried depression 20 km east of Site A is the impact crater, and the layer is thickest near it because most droplets fell close to their source. The nickel came from the meteorite itself. Shocked quartz is absent because the impact struck limestone, which contains almost no quartz. Because the droplets cooled in the near-vacuum of the upper atmosphere, the spherules should be free of gas bubbles and should contain microscopic droplets of nickel-iron metal.

Scientist 2
The layer was produced by an explosive eruption in the volcanic field 300 km west of Site A. The silica content of the spherules, 70%, matches that of the volcanic glass found in that field and is far higher than that of melted limestone. Droplets of molten rock thrown from the vent cooled into spheres as they fell into the sea. Winds carried the fine droplets eastward, and once they were in the water, currents flowing into the basin at Site A concentrated them there; that is why the layer is thickest at Site A rather than near the volcanoes. The nickel was carried into the magma by sulfur-rich fluids, which are known to concentrate nickel. The buried depression is a sinkhole that formed when a layer of salt beneath the seafloor dissolved. Because the droplets formed from gas-rich magma, the spherules should contain many small gas bubbles.

The charcoal from the 1.0 g trial at pH 7 was collected on a filter at 60 min, rinsed with 50 mL of water, dried at 105 °C, and added to a fresh 100 mL portion of 50 mg/L dye solution at pH 7. R is dominant to the susceptible allele, S: mosquitoes of genotype RR or RS survive exposure to the insecticide, and SS mosquitoes are killed by it. In a population in which mating is random, if the frequency of the R allele is p and the frequency of the S allele is q = 1 − p, the fraction of the population with genotype SS is expected to be q², and the fraction that is resistant (RR or RS) is expected to be 1 − q².

A town at the western end of a river valley has sprayed the insecticide inside its houses every June for the past 12 years. The insecticide has never been used elsewhere in the valley. Because SS mosquitoes are killed during spraying, the frequency of R in the town rises sharply each June and then declines over the following months as mosquitoes move in from unsprayed areas. In one week in September, researchers set light traps overnight at six sites in the valley: at the town's edge (0 km) and at 2, 5, 10, 20, and 40 km east of the town along the river. From each site, 200 adult mosquitoes were collected and genotyped, and the frequency of the R allele was calculated as the number of R alleles divided by the total number of alleles (400 per site). A thin layer of tiny glass spheres (spherules) occurs in marine sedimentary rock at three sites in a coastal region. At Site A the layer is 3.0 cm thick; at Site B, 200 km north of Site A, it is 1.2 cm thick; and at Site C, 500 km north of Site A, it is 0.4 cm thick. At all three sites the layer lies between the same two fossil-bearing limestone beds, so it was deposited at the same time everywhere. The spherules are 0.1 mm to 1 mm in diameter and are about 70% silica (SiO2) by mass. They contain about 2,000 parts per million (ppm) of nickel; typical rock of Earth's continental crust contains about 80 ppm. No grains of shocked quartz (quartz with the microscopic fracture planes produced only by extremely high pressure) have been found in the layer. A field of extinct volcanoes lies 300 km west of Site A, and a circular depression 4 km across, now buried under younger sediment, has been detected beneath the seafloor 20 km east of Site A. Two scientists discuss how the layer formed.

Scientist 1
The layer was produced by the impact of a nickel-rich meteorite. The impact melted the rock at the point of impact and sprayed molten droplets high into the atmosphere; the droplets became spheres as they cooled in flight and rained down over the region. The buried depression 20 km east of Site A is the impact crater, and the layer is thickest near it because most droplets fell close to their source. The nickel came from the meteorite itself. Shocked quartz is absent because the impact struck limestone, which contains almost no quartz. Because the droplets cooled in the near-vacuum of the upper atmosphere, the spherules should be free of gas bubbles and should contain microscopic droplets of nickel-iron metal.

Scientist 2
The layer was produced by an explosive eruption in the volcanic field 300 km west of Site A. The silica content of the spherules, 70%, matches that of the volcanic glass found in that field and is far higher than that of melted limestone. Droplets of molten rock thrown from the vent cooled into spheres as they fell into the sea. Winds carried the fine droplets eastward, and once they were in the water, currents flowing into the basin at Site A concentrated them there; that is why the layer is thickest at Site A rather than near the volcanoes. The nickel was carried into the magma by sulfur-rich fluids, which are known to concentrate nickel. The buried depression is a sinkhole that formed when a layer of salt beneath the seafloor dissolved. Because the droplets formed from gas-rich magma, the spherules should contain many small gas bubbles.

A thin layer of tiny glass spheres (spherules) occurs in marine sedimentary rock at three sites in a coastal region. At Site A the layer is 3.0 cm thick; at Site B, 200 km north of Site A, it is 1.2 cm thick; and at Site C, 500 km north of Site A, it is 0.4 cm thick. At all three sites the layer lies between the same two fossil-bearing limestone beds, so it was deposited at the same time everywhere. The spherules are 0.1 mm to 1 mm in diameter and are about 70% silica (SiO2) by mass. They contain about 2,000 parts per million (ppm) of nickel; typical rock of Earth's continental crust contains about 80 ppm. No grains of shocked quartz (quartz with the microscopic fracture planes produced only by extremely high pressure) have been found in the layer. A field of extinct volcanoes lies 300 km west of Site A, and a circular depression 4 km across, now buried under younger sediment, has been detected beneath the seafloor 20 km east of Site A. Two scientists discuss how the layer formed.

Scientist 1
The layer was produced by the impact of a nickel-rich meteorite. The impact melted the rock at the point of impact and sprayed molten droplets high into the atmosphere; the droplets became spheres as they cooled in flight and rained down over the region. The buried depression 20 km east of Site A is the impact crater, and the layer is thickest near it because most droplets fell close to their source. The nickel came from the meteorite itself. Shocked quartz is absent because the impact struck limestone, which contains almost no quartz. Because the droplets cooled in the near-vacuum of the upper atmosphere, the spherules should be free of gas bubbles and should contain microscopic droplets of nickel-iron metal.

Scientist 2
The layer was produced by an explosive eruption in the volcanic field 300 km west of Site A. The silica content of the spherules, 70%, matches that of the volcanic glass found in that field and is far higher than that of melted limestone. Droplets of molten rock thrown from the vent cooled into spheres as they fell into the sea. Winds carried the fine droplets eastward, and once they were in the water, currents flowing into the basin at Site A concentrated them there; that is why the layer is thickest at Site A rather than near the volcanoes. The nickel was carried into the magma by sulfur-rich fluids, which are known to concentrate nickel. The buried depression is a sinkhole that formed when a layer of salt beneath the seafloor dissolved. Because the droplets formed from gas-rich magma, the spherules should contain many small gas bubbles.
question: Suppose the spherules were examined under a microscope and found to contain many small gas bubbles. This finding would be most consistent with the viewpoint of:

options.A: Scientist 2, because gas bubbles form when droplets of gas-rich magma cool.
options.B: Scientist 2, because gas bubbles would indicate that the droplets were concentrated by ocean currents.
options.C: Scientist 1, because gas bubbles would indicate that the droplets were sprayed from an impact crater.
options.D: Scientist 1, because gas bubbles form when droplets cool in the near-vacuum of the upper atmosphere.

Activated charcoal removes dissolved dyes from water by adsorption: dye molecules stick to the charcoal's surface. Students measured the removal of a blue dye from water. In each trial, a flask containing 100 mL of a 50 mg/L dye solution was placed in a water bath at 25 °C and stirred, and a measured mass of powdered activated charcoal was added at time 0. At 10, 20, 30, 45, and 60 min, a 2 mL sample was withdrawn, passed through a filter with 0.45 µm pores, and placed in a spectrophotometer, which measured the sample's absorbance of light at a wavelength of 590 nm (the wavelength the dye absorbs most strongly). The dye concentration of each sample was determined from a calibration curve prepared from dye solutions of known concentration at pH 7. Percent removal was calculated as the percent of the original 50 mg/L that was no longer present in solution.

Experiment 1
Trials were performed at pH 7 with 0.5 g, 1.0 g, or 2.0 g of charcoal. The results are shown in Figure 1 (solid lines).

Experiment 2
Trials were performed with 1.0 g of charcoal in dye solutions adjusted to pH 3 or pH 11 by adding a few drops of hydrochloric acid or sodium hydroxide solution. The results are shown in Figure 1 (dashed lines). The students later found that, at the same dye concentration, a solution at pH 11 has an absorbance at 590 nm that is 15% lower than that of a solution at pH 7, and that the absorbance at pH 3 is the same as at pH 7.

Experiment 3
The charcoal from the 1.0 g trial at pH 7 was collected on a filter at 60 min, rinsed with 50 mL of water, dried at 105 °C, and added to a fresh 100 mL portion of 50 mg/L dye solution at pH 7. After 60 min, 61% of the dye had been removed. When the same charcoal was collected, rinsed, dried, and used a third time, 45% of the dye had been removed after 60 min.

Astronomers monitored the brightness of a Sun-like star, K-31, for five years. Every 11.3 days the star dims by a few percent for about 6 hours and then returns to its normal brightness. Four features of these dimming events are notable: (1) each event is deeper when the star is observed in blue light than when it is observed in red light; (2) the depth of the events has decreased gradually, from 4.0% in the first year of monitoring to 3.0% in the fifth year; (3) the interval between events has remained 11.3 days to within a few minutes; and (4) spectra of the star show no periodic Doppler shift larger than 5 m/s, the smallest shift the instruments can detect. Three scientists offer explanations.

Scientist 1
A planet orbits K-31 with a period of 11.3 days and passes in front of the star once each orbit. The planet is surrounded by an extended hazy atmosphere. The haze scatters blue light more strongly than red light, so the planet blocks more blue light and the events are deeper in blue. The planet's mass is small, so the Doppler shift it produces in the star's spectrum is below the detection limit. A second, more distant planet is slowly tilting the first planet's orbit, so that a shrinking fraction of the planet's disk crosses the star each orbit; this is why the events are becoming shallower.

Scientist 2
A cloud of dust orbits K-31 with a period of 11.3 days. The cloud is debris from a small icy body that broke apart. Dust grains scatter blue light more strongly than red light, which explains the color difference. The cloud's mass is far too small to move the star, so no Doppler shift is expected. The cloud is slowly spreading out along its orbit; a more spread-out cloud blocks less light at any one moment, which is why the events are becoming shallower.

Scientist 3
No body orbits K-31. The star rotates once every 11.3 days and carries a large dark spot, a cooler region of its surface. Each time rotation brings the spot into view, the star appears dimmer. Because a cooler surface emits proportionally less blue light than red light, the events are deeper in blue. The spot is gradually shrinking, so the events are becoming shallower. Spots of this kind drift slowly toward a star's equator, where the star rotates slightly faster, so the interval between events should shorten by several hours over the coming years.
question: If Scientist 2's explanation of why the events are becoming shallower is correct, the duration of each event should, over the coming years:

options.A: remain the same, because the cloud's orbital period is unchanged.
options.B: decrease, because a spreading cloud moves faster along its orbit.
options.C: increase, because a more spread-out cloud takes longer to pass in front of the star.
options.D: decrease, because a spreading cloud contains fewer dust grains.

Activated charcoal removes dissolved dyes from water by adsorption: dye molecules stick to the charcoal's surface. Students measured the removal of a blue dye from water. In each trial, a flask containing 100 mL of a 50 mg/L dye solution was placed in a water bath at 25 °C and stirred, and a measured mass of powdered activated charcoal was added at time 0. At 10, 20, 30, 45, and 60 min, a 2 mL sample was withdrawn, passed through a filter with 0.45 µm pores, and placed in a spectrophotometer, which measured the sample's absorbance of light at a wavelength of 590 nm (the wavelength the dye absorbs most strongly). The dye concentration of each sample was determined from a calibration curve prepared from dye solutions of known concentration at pH 7. Percent removal was calculated as the percent of the original 50 mg/L that was no longer present in solution.

Experiment 1
Trials were performed at pH 7 with 0.5 g, 1.0 g, or 2.0 g of charcoal. The results are shown in Figure 1 (solid lines).

Experiment 2
Trials were performed with 1.0 g of charcoal in dye solutions adjusted to pH 3 or pH 11 by adding a few drops of hydrochloric acid or sodium hydroxide solution. The results are shown in Figure 1 (dashed lines). The students later found that, at the same dye concentration, a solution at pH 11 has an absorbance at 590 nm that is 15% lower than that of a solution at pH 7, and that the absorbance at pH 3 is the same as at pH 7.

Experiment 3
The charcoal from the 1.0 g trial at pH 7 was collected on a filter at 60 min, rinsed with 50 mL of water, dried at 105 °C, and added to a fresh 100 mL portion of 50 mg/L dye solution at pH 7. After 60 min, 61% of the dye had been removed. When the same charcoal was collected, rinsed, dried, and used a third time, 45% of the dye had been removed after 60 min.

Dissolved oxygen (DO) is oxygen gas held in solution in water. The greatest DO concentration that seawater can hold when it is in equilibrium with the air, called the saturation concentration, depends on the water's temperature. For the salinity of the bay described here, the saturation concentration is 9.0 mg/L at 10 °C, 8.1 mg/L at 15 °C, 7.4 mg/L at 20 °C, and 6.7 mg/L at 25 °C. The percent saturation of a water sample is its DO concentration divided by the saturation concentration at the sample's temperature, multiplied by 100. Water with a DO concentration below 2.0 mg/L is called hypoxic; most fish and crabs cannot survive in hypoxic water for long.

In late summer, researchers lowered a probe from a boat at two stations in a coastal bay. Station A was in the open outer bay, 3 km from the mouth of a river. Station B was in the inner bay, 0.5 km from the river mouth and sheltered from the wind by a peninsula. At each station the probe recorded water temperature and DO concentration every 5 m from the surface to a depth of 30 m. At Station B the probe malfunctioned at a depth of 15 m, so no readings were recorded at that depth. Figure 1 shows DO concentration versus depth, and Figure 2 shows water temperature versus depth, at the two stations.

passage:
Astronomers monitored the brightness of a Sun-like star, K-31, for five years. Every 11.3 days the star dims by a few percent for about 6 hours and then returns to its normal brightness. Four features of these dimming events are notable: (1) each event is deeper when the star is observed in blue light than when it is observed in red light; (2) the depth of the events has decreased gradually, from 4.0% in the first year of monitoring to 3.0% in the fifth year; (3) the interval between events has remained 11.3 days to within a few minutes; and (4) spectra of the star show no periodic Doppler shift larger than 5 m/s, the smallest shift the instruments can detect. Three scientists offer explanations.

Scientist 1
A planet orbits K-31 with a period of 11.3 days and passes in front of the star once each orbit. The planet is surrounded by an extended hazy atmosphere. The haze scatters blue light more strongly than red light, so the planet blocks more blue light and the events are deeper in blue. The planet's mass is small, so the Doppler shift it produces in the star's spectrum is below the detection limit. A second, more distant planet is slowly tilting the first planet's orbit, so that a shrinking fraction of the planet's disk crosses the star each orbit; this is why the events are becoming shallower.

Scientist 2
A cloud of dust orbits K-31 with a period of 11.3 days. The cloud is debris from a small icy body that broke apart. Dust grains scatter blue light more strongly than red light, which explains the color difference. The cloud's mass is far too small to move the star, so no Doppler shift is expected. The cloud is slowly spreading out along its orbit; a more spread-out cloud blocks less light at any one moment, which is why the events are becoming shallower.

Scientist 3
No body orbits K-31. The star rotates once every 11.3 days and carries a large dark spot, a cooler region of its surface. Each time rotation brings the spot into view, the star appears dimmer. Because a cooler surface emits proportionally less blue light than red light, the events are deeper in blue. The spot is gradually shrinking, so the events are becoming shallower. Spots of this kind drift slowly toward a star's equator, where the star rotates slightly faster, so the interval between events should shorten by several hours over the coming years.
question: Which of the following observations would best test the prediction Scientist 3 makes about the interval between events?

options.A: Measuring the depth of the events in infrared light as well as in blue light over the next several years.
options.B: Timing the events over the next several years to see whether the interval shortens.
options.C: Measuring the star's brightness between events over the next several years.
options.D: Searching the star's brightness record for a second, shallower series of events.
